svg.text: COPPER SIDE, mirrored: what you see when you cut the tracks
20 × 29 holes · cut to 50.8 × 73.7 mm · 18 cuts · 3 links · 2 standoff holes (2.5 mm, for M2.5 nylon standoffs)
The Pico, its link to the Pi, and three footswitches. The small case’s first control board.
D4 1N5817 — band towards VSYS, the right-hand lead
Connectors (pin 1 is the large filled square)
D3 → Core breakout, JST-XH 4-way (B4B-XH-A): 1 GND · 2 Pico TX (GP0) → Pi
RXD, pin 10 · 3 Pico RX (GP1) ← Pi TXD, pin 8 · 4 +5 V hold
FS 1 GND · 2 FS1 GP10 · 3 FS2 GP11 · 4 FS3 GP12
GND reaches the root through D3 only (Core breakout).
The control board with everything but the link and the footswitches left
off. The Pico sits where it sits on that board, relative to its own strips,
and the footswitch pins are the same: GP10, GP11 and GP12, physical pins 14,
FS is the first four pins of the map’s C4, in its order: GND, FS1, FS2, FS3.
Each switch joins its pin to GND. No resistors: the Pico’s own pull-ups hold
the pins high, and the firmware turns them on.
The 100 nF across each switch is soldered on the switch’s two lugs, not
The diode is how the Pico keeps running when the Pi reboots: D3’s 5 V is the
Pi’s pin 4, and the band faces VSYS. If the Pico’s present lead already has
a 1N5817 in it, take that one out: two in series cost the Pico 0.3 V for
Cut every strip between the Pico’s two rows at the marked hole, except its
four ground rows; then the strip between the diode’s leads, and D3’s 5 V
docs/build-footswitches.md is the wiring from FS to the switches’ lugs.
The USB console lead and the Debug Probe plug into the Pico’s own sockets.

Red ✕: cut the track at that hole (red bar: cut between two holes). Lines: wire links on the component side (green carries ground). Strips tinted green carry ground, red a supply, amber 3.3 V. White circles: standoff holes; dashed: what the standoff covers.
